newsitem.title: Kenya: Kenya protest leaders released after state rally.
newsitem.headline: Kenya protest leaders released after state rally.

text.p: Four Kenyan opposition parliamentarians were released from house arrest on Sunday at the end of a state rally they had threatened to disrupt, an opposition leader said.
President Daniel arap Moi, defying opposition demands, told the rally in Nairobi's Uhuru Park there could be no constitutional change before elections later this year.
Opposition and church leaders scorned Moi's speech and vowed to continue mass protests in support implementation of a package of constitutional reforms before the elections.

"The intention was not to arrest us. The intention was to prevent us getting to Uhuru Park," Paul Muite, an activist in the unregistered Safina party, told Reuters by telephone. He added that police had withdrawn from around his house.

Muite said security forces also allowed National Development Party leader Raila Odinga, FORD-Asili chairman Kenneth Matiba and FORD-Kenya chairman Michael Kijana Wamalwa to leave their homes after the rally.

"We would again express our concern and disappointment that the government has responded by curtailing people's right to freedom of association, which is guaranteed in international law," said Mark Ogle, spokesman for human rights group Amnesty International.

Moi told a crowd of around 10,000 at the rally: "The current atmosphere is not conducive to meaningful discussion on subjects such as the constitution. Such discussion can only be held meaningfully after the general elections.
"A commission will then be appointed that will take into account all interested parties."

The heavily-guarded rally passed without incident but in Nairobi's run-down outer business district security forces battled looters in a renewed flare-up of the rioting that paralysed the capital on Saturday, eyewitnesses said.
Scores of residents set tyres on fire to hamper police access and looted shops. Unconfirmed reports spoke of police beating rioters and making about 10 arrests.
But the unrest was not on the scale of that on Saturday, which brought Nairobi to a standstill on Saturday and caused one death as security forces broke up a banned opposition rally.

Moi, addressing the annual Madaraka (Self Rule) Day rally on Sunday, said the Public Order Act used to regulate public meetings would be replaced by a new bill, but gave no details of how it would differ.
"A new legislation entitled the Peaceful Assemblies Bill will soon be presented for debate in parliament. This will replace the Public Order Act," he said.
But opposition and church leaders said they mistrusted Moi's plans and would continue to press for constitutional reform even if it meant defying the law.

"This is too little, too late. The minimum reforms we have specified are an absolute minimum, so the mass action will continue. We intend to go to Kisumu and Mombasa to hold rallies and we will not apply for licences," Muite said.
"Moi is trying to hoodwink Kenyans. This is not enough. We are going to press for minimum constitutional reforms before the elections," NDP secretary general Charles Maranga told Reuters.
President Moi must call elections by the end of 1997 pitting the ruling Kenya African National Union (KANU) against an opposition undermined by ethnic, political and personal disputes.
Opposition, church and human rights groups under the National Convention Assembly (NCA) umbrella argue that fair elections are impossible under a constitution designed for a single-party state.

The NCA wants six pre-independence laws scrapped including the Public Order Act that regulates public meetings. They also demand an independent electoral commission and greater access to state-controlled Kenyan radio and television.
"Granting constitutional change after the election is like giving medicine to a person already dead," Timothy Njoya, a moderator in the Presbyterian Church of East Africa said.

Moi came to power in 1978 on the death of Kenya's first president Jomo Kenyatta. Kenya's first multi-party elections were held in 1992, when Moi defeated opposition contenders amid charges of rigging and widespread violence.
